fixes.explanation: The verse says, "the nations scatter when You rise." Just before that, "The peoples flee the thunder of Your voice…" So when the LORD rises, the nations scatter and the peoples flee. I'd scatter too.

That's it, baker. The verse says, "He has filled Zion with justice and righteousness." The same verse says the LORD is exalted, for He dwells on high. Filled is a big word, too, because Zion isn't getting a sprinkle of it. It's getting a full measure.

Yes. Isaiah says, "The treaty has been broken…" The same verse says the highways are deserted and travel has ceased. The verse doesn't say who broke it, only that it's broken. Empty roads and a broken treaty, all in one verse.

That's right. Isaiah says, "…the witnesses are despised…" The same verse says the treaty has been broken and "…human life is disregarded." Despised is a heavy word, and I think this verse hurts to read.
The verse doesn't say they're missing. It says "…the witnesses are despised…" Despised is about how they're treated. That's the picture Isaiah paints.

Yes. The LORD says, "Your breath is a fire that will consume you." He says it to the ones who conceive chaff and give birth to stubble. It's a hard verse, so I'll say it plainly: the fire is called their own breath.
Guiding isn't what this fire does. The LORD says, "Your breath is a fire that will consume you." Consume means burn up. The same verse says, "You conceive chaff; you give birth to stubble."
Yes. The LORD says, "The peoples will be burned to ashes, like thorns cut down and set ablaze." It's a serious verse. The verse before it says, "You conceive chaff; you give birth to stubble."
Yes. Isaiah says, "the mountain fortress will be his refuge…" That's about the one who walks righteously, who will dwell on the heights. A fortress up there sounds a lot better than a leaky tent.

Yes. The text says, "his food will be provided and his water assured." Provided and assured are the words Isaiah uses for his food and water. That same verse puts him on the heights, with the mountain fortress as his refuge.
No priest here, friend. A priest in robes would look sharp, I'll give you that. But Isaiah says, "Your eyes will see the King in His beauty…" and the King is who's in view.
Good thought, but no. Isaiah says, "Your eyes will see the King in His beauty…" There's not a mantle anywhere in that line.
Isaiah says the opposite. He says, "You will no longer see the insolent, a people whose speech is unintelligible…" No longer means they won't see them anymore. So the statement has it backwards.

Yes. Isaiah says, "…the Majestic One, our LORD, will be for us a place of rivers and wide canals…" The place isn't a king or a city on its own. The LORD Himself is that place for them. The next verse says, "For the LORD is our Judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our King."

Solomon isn't named anywhere in this passage. Isaiah says, "…the Majestic One, our LORD, will be for us a place of rivers and wide canals…" A king does come up in verse 22, and it's the LORD: "the LORD is our King."

David isn't named anywhere in this passage. Isaiah says, "…the Majestic One, our LORD, will be for us a place of rivers and wide canals…" A king does come up in verse 22, and it's the LORD: "the LORD is our King."
Yes. Isaiah says, "It is He who will save us." The LORD is their Judge, their lawgiver and their King. Three titles, and the verse lands on one promise.
Watching isn't in this verse, friend. Isaiah says, "It is He who will save us." That's the promise that follows Judge, lawgiver and King. Saving, not watching, is what the LORD does here.
That's what Isaiah says: "…even the lame will carry off plunder." It comes right after he says an abundance of spoils will be divided. The lame are the ones he names as carrying it off.
I like the guess, baker, but the elders aren't in this verse. Isaiah says, "…even the lame will carry off plunder." The lame are the ones he names.
Strangers are a fair guess, but they don't show up in this verse. Isaiah says, "…even the lame will carry off plunder." The lame are the ones he names, so that's the answer.
Yes. Isaiah says, "The people who dwell there will be forgiven of iniquity." That's how the chapter ends. Right before it, he says no resident of Zion will say, "I am sick."
Written down is a fair guess, but that isn't what Isaiah says. He says, "The people who dwell there will be forgiven of iniquity." Forgiven is where the chapter ends, so that's the one.
Passed down sounds like a family recipe, baker, but the verse doesn't say that. Isaiah says, "The people who dwell there will be forgiven of iniquity." Forgiven is where the chapter ends.
